**Internal Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Summary and Recommendation**

We recommend that we invest the next six to eight weeks in improving utilisation of our existing GPU fleet before committing to any new hardware purchases. Our current utilisation data suggests we are leaving meaningful capacity on the table, and the cost of a focused efficiency effort is a small fraction of the capital required for new machines. If utilisation work stalls or demand continues to grow past what we can recover, we should revisit procurement with better data in hand — and we should treat that as a likely follow-on rather than a failure of this plan.

**Where We Stand**

Our fleet of eight A100-class nodes currently averages around 40% utilisation, with significant variance across the week. Peak demand on weekday afternoons pushes us near saturation, which is where our latency complaints originate, while nights and weekends sit largely idle. The pattern is not one of insufficient aggregate capacity but of poor temporal matching: batch training jobs, interactive inference, and ad-hoc experimentation all compete for the same nodes at the same hours, and nothing systematically shifts flexible workloads into the quiet windows.

The cost picture reinforces this. A new node would cost roughly $180K upfront plus power, cooling, and rack space, and our facilities team has flagged that provisioning would take eight to ten weeks once ordered. By contrast, the utilisation work is mostly engineering time we already control: a proper job scheduler with priority queues, batching of inference requests, quantisation of our two highest-volume models, and moving nightly retraining into off-peak windows. None of this is exotic. Teams across the industry routinely recover 30 to 50 percentage points of utilisation through exactly these measures.

**Latency and Reliability Considerations**

The latency argument deserves honest treatment, because it is the strongest case for buying. Our interactive inference p99 has crept from 400ms to nearly a second at peak, and that is a real product problem. But adding a node treats the symptom unevenly — it would relieve peak pressure while adding idle capacity everywhere else. Batching and quantisation attack the same problem at a fraction of the cost, and a scheduler with workload classes would protect interactive traffic from batch jobs that currently trample it. If we cannot get p99 back under 600ms with these measures, that becomes concrete evidence for procurement.

Reliability cuts the other way, and we should say so plainly. Eight nodes is already a thin margin; a single hardware failure removes 12.5% of our fleet, and our maintenance windows are becoming harder to schedule. Buying more hardware genuinely improves fault tolerance in a way that utilisation work cannot. This is the one dimension where the efficiency argument is weakest, and it is the primary reason we should not rule out purchase indefinitely — only defer it until we know our true steady-state need.

**Opportunity Cost and Reversibility**

The opportunity cost of buying now is not just the $180K. It is the engineering time diverted to integration and facilities work, the commitment of budget that might be better spent after the next model generation lands (hardware prices per unit of compute keep falling, and our vendor has hinted at next-gen availability within two quarters), and the risk of locking in capacity sized to a demand curve we do not yet understand. Utilisation work, by contrast, is highly reversible: a scheduler can be reconfigured, quantisation can be rolled back per-model, and nothing we build is wasted even if we later buy hardware, since better scheduling makes any future fleet cheaper to run.

Buying is also not fully reversible. Once capital is committed and rack space provisioned, the sunk cost exerts pressure to keep using machines even when demand shifts, and our finance team has been explicit that hardware write-downs are unwelcome.

**Uncertainty**

We are genuinely uncertain about demand trajectory. If the new product line ships in Q3, inference load could double, and no amount of scheduling will absorb that. We are also uncertain about how much utilisation we can actually recover — our 40% figure may understate contention, since queueing delays mean the fleet feels more saturated than the numbers suggest. We will know more within a month of deploying the scheduler.

**Next Steps**

We propose starting the utilisation work immediately, setting a checkpoint at eight weeks with explicit latency and throughput targets, and pre-drafting the procurement request so that if we do need to buy, we lose no time. This keeps the option open without paying for it today.

**Internal Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Local AI hardware — expansion vs. utilisation
**Status:** Recommendation for discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past six weeks we've looked closely at how our local inference cluster is actually being used, and the picture is more nuanced than the "we're out of capacity" framing that has driven recent conversations. I want to lay out the trade-offs as we see them and make a recommendation, while being honest about where our confidence is thin.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward on its face. Our p99 latency on the shared inference pool has degraded noticeably during peak hours, and two teams have deferred experiments because they couldn't get predictable access to accelerators. Latency matters to us in a concrete way: the interactive features that depend on our models degrade perceptibly above certain response thresholds, and we've crossed those thresholds more often this quarter than last. There's also a reliability argument. Our current fleet has no meaningful spare capacity, so a single node failure during business hours means degraded service rather than graceful failover. Buying hardware fixes both problems immediately and unconditionally.

But the utilisation data complicates the story. Average utilisation across the fleet sits around 40%, and even our busiest nodes rarely sustain above 65% outside of scheduled batch windows. A meaningful fraction of our capacity is consumed by idle-but-reserved notebooks, poorly batched small jobs, and models served at default precision when quantised versions would be indistinguishable for our purposes. If we could move average utilisation to 60% — an ambitious but not unprecedented target — we would effectively add the equivalent of half our current fleet without spending anything on capital. The cost of that path is mostly engineering time: better scheduling, a proper queue with priorities, batching improvements, and the political work of taking away informal reservations that teams have come to rely on.

The opportunity cost cuts both ways, and this is where the decision gets genuinely hard. Money spent on hardware is money not spent on hiring, on the evaluation tooling several teams have asked for, or simply held in reserve given the uncertainty in our funding outlook. Conversely, engineering time spent on utilisation work is time not spent on product features, and there's a real risk we invest two engineers for a quarter and capture less of the efficiency gain than we project. Utilisation improvements also tend to decay: scheduling discipline erodes, new teams arrive with new habits, and the queue we build today may be the bottleneck everyone resents in a year.

Reversibility is the strongest argument in favour of the utilisation path. Hardware purchases are largely irreversible at our scale — depreciation is fast in this market, resale values for used accelerators are poor, and a purchase made for this year's workload mix may be poorly matched to next year's. Process and software improvements, by contrast, can be adjusted, abandoned, or built upon cheaply. If we improve utilisation and still fall short, we will have lost some time but gained a much sharper picture of what we actually need to buy, and any future purchase will be better specified because of it. The reverse is not true: if we buy hardware and the demand was softer than it appeared, we're stuck with the bill and the rack space.

There is one exception we should carve out. The reliability gap — the absence of failover capacity — is not something utilisation work can responsibly solve, and a single-node outage taking down interactive features is a reputational risk we shouldn't carry into the next quarter. A minimal redundancy purchase, roughly one additional node rather than a fleet expansion, addresses that specific exposure at a fraction of the cost of the full expansion proposal.

My recommendation, then: defer the large hardware purchase for two quarters, fund a focused utilisation effort with clear, measurable targets (average utilisation above 55%, p99 latency back under our interactive threshold, a functioning priority queue), and approve the single-node redundancy purchase now. Revisit expansion at the end of that period with real data in hand.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Our utilisation measurements come from a monitoring setup we ourselves describe as approximate, and demand forecasts for the second half of the year are little more than informed guesses. If a major new initiative lands on us, this recommendation could be wrong within weeks. But the plan is designed to fail safely: if utilisation work underdelivers, we buy hardware with better information; if it overdelivers, we've saved the capital entirely. That asymmetry is the strongest argument for patience.

Happy to walk through the numbers at Thursday's session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

---

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for about six weeks now. Peak-hour GPU utilisation regularly exceeds 85%, queue times during the afternoon window have crept from seconds into the tens of seconds, and two of our internal customers have started asking whether they should route around us entirely. The obvious question on the table is whether we should buy more hardware. My recommendation, after working through the numbers and talking to the teams affected, is that we should not — not yet. We should first invest four to six weeks in improving utilisation of what we own, and hold the purchase decision open until we see what that yields.

The case for buying is real, and I don't want to minimise it. Our latency problem is genuine, and latency is the kind of failure that erodes trust quietly: nobody files an incident when a batch job takes ninety seconds instead of twenty, but people stop building on your platform when it feels slow. New hardware would solve that immediately and would be the lowest-effort path to a comfortable margin. It would also give us headroom for the two new model deployments planned for next quarter, which we currently have no realistic way to schedule.

But the case against buying right now is stronger, and it rests on three observations.

First, our utilisation is uneven in ways that suggest waste rather than genuine scarcity. A meaningful share of our GPU-hours goes to a handful of long-running jobs that hold memory but compute intermittently — development workloads, mostly, belonging to teams that provisioned capacity months ago and never released it. We have no meaningful quota system and no reclamation process. Some fraction of our "scarcity" is simply stale allocation. Before we spend capital, we should know how much of the demand is real.

Second, the cost asymmetry matters. A purchase is a large, largely irreversible commitment: depreciation begins immediately, and if our workload profile shifts — as it plausibly will if the batch-processing migration lands — we could find ourselves owning hardware optimised for a problem we no longer have. The utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we'd spend anyway, and nearly every piece of it (quotas, better batching, a scheduling queue, observability into per-team consumption) is valuable regardless of what we decide later. In option terms, improving utilisation is cheap and reversible; buying is expensive and sticky. When two paths both plausibly lead to a good outcome, the reversible one deserves the first attempt.

Third, there's the opportunity cost of the purchase itself. The capital and, more importantly, the team attention that procurement, racking, and integrating new hardware would consume would come directly out of the reliability work we've been deferring — the checkpointing improvements and the failover testing that would let us survive a node loss without dropping requests. Right now a single hardware failure during peak hours would be genuinely painful. Resilience to that failure mode is worth more to our internal customers than a lower p99, and it's the thing we can only get by doing the unglamorous work.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. It's possible that the utilisation gains are illusory — that the stale allocations turn out to be a small fraction, and that demand is growing fast enough that we hit the same wall in October regardless. It's also possible that the scheduling work introduces its own latency and complexity, and that a queue that adds jitter is worse than a slightly overprovisioned cluster. And there's a political dimension I can't quantify: if we spend six weeks optimising and then buy hardware anyway, we will have spent six weeks. If the growth curve is steep, that delay has a real cost. My judgement is that the probability of meaningful waste is high enough, and the cost of the investigation low enough, that the expected value favours waiting — but I'd put maybe seventy percent confidence on that, not ninety.

Concretely, I propose we implement per-team quotas and a simple request queue, instrument per-workload utilisation properly, and reconvene in six weeks with data. If peak utilisation on *real* demand is still above 80% after reclamation, we buy, and we'll do so with a much better model of what we actually need — which may well be less than the current panic suggests.

Happy to argue about this Thursday.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Local AI hardware strategy for the next two quarters

**Status: Recommendation at end**

Over the past month we've been asked, informally but repeatedly, whether we should purchase additional local inference hardware or invest in raising the utilisation of the machines we already own. The question sounds like a simple procurement decision, but it isn't, and I want to lay out our reasoning before we commit either way.

Let me start with the case that everyone finds intuitive: we're busy, our GPUs are busy, therefore we need more GPUs. The intuition is half right. Our four A100 nodes currently run at roughly 68% average utilisation, but that average hides the real problem. Peak demand — the morning batch window and the afternoon evaluation runs — pushes us to saturation, and during those windows queue latency for internal teams has crept from minutes to over an hour. The rest of the day, the same hardware idles at 30% or less. So the pain is real, but it is a *shape* problem as much as a *volume* problem. Buying more hardware would fix the peaks; it would also deepen the troughs, and the troughs are where our money quietly evaporates.

On cost, the numbers are sobering. A fifth node would cost approximately £180k upfront, plus power, cooling, and the operational overhead of another machine to patch, monitor, and eventually depreciate. Amortised over an expected four-year life, that's meaningful money for a team our size — money that would otherwise fund a hire, or two quarters of contractor support, or simply stay in reserve. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is mostly an investment of engineering time: better job scheduling, a shared queue with sensible priorities, quantised model variants for workloads that don't need full precision, and consolidating the long-tail of small jobs that currently each reserve an entire GPU for hours while using a fraction of its memory. We estimate six to eight engineer-weeks to do this properly. That is not free, but it is an order of magnitude cheaper, and it is work we would benefit from regardless of what we later buy.

Latency deserves honest treatment. Scheduling improvements will reduce *average* wait times substantially, but they cannot conjure capacity that doesn't exist at peak. If the team's trajectory continues — and our request volume has grown about 15% month over month — better utilisation buys us perhaps two to three quarters of headroom, not a permanent solution. There is also a risk that a smarter scheduler introduces its own failure modes: preemption bugs, jobs that starve, subtle fairness problems that erode trust in the shared queue. We should not pretend this is risk-free engineering.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy; if a node fails today, we lose a quarter of our capacity, which is genuinely painful. But it also means more components to fail and a larger maintenance surface. Better utilisation, done well, actually improves reliability in a softer sense: a well-instrumented, well-understood fleet of four machines is easier to operate than a hastily integrated fifth, and the monitoring we'd build to schedule jobs efficiently would also surface degradation earlier.

The opportunity cost and reversibility considerations are, to me, the decisive ones. Capital spent on hardware is largely irreversible at our scale — resale values for used accelerators are poor, and the market moves fast enough that a node bought today may be unremarkable in eighteen months. Engineering time invested in scheduling and instrumentation is reversible in the sense that it compounds: the tooling, the telemetry, and the operational discipline all transfer to whatever fleet we eventually run, including a larger one. If we later decide to buy, we will do so with better data about our true demand curve, and we may find we need less than we feared — or we may shift some workloads to hosted APIs for the spiky, latency-tolerant jobs and never need the fifth node at all.

**Recommendation:** Do not buy the fifth node now. Spend the next six weeks on utilisation work — scheduling, quantisation, and instrumentation — with a defined target of keeping p95 queue latency under fifteen minutes. Revisit procurement at the end of that period with real measurements in hand. If peak demand still exceeds capacity after the low-hanging fruit is picked, we buy, and we will buy with confidence rather than anxiety.

The main uncertainty I want to flag: if a major project lands in the next month requiring dedicated capacity, this analysis changes, and we should treat that as a trigger to revisit rather than a reason to improvise.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's sync.

**Internal Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we invest the next six to eight weeks in improving utilisation of our existing GPU fleet before committing to any new hardware purchases. Our current utilisation sits at roughly 35–40% of available compute hours, and the cheapest capacity we can acquire is the capacity we already own but fail to use. If, after a genuine improvement effort, we still face sustained queueing during peak windows, we should then buy — and we should buy with a specific workload profile in mind rather than a vague sense that "we'll need it eventually."

**The current situation**

Our fleet of eight A100-class cards serves three constituencies: the inference service backing our customer-facing features, the fine-tuning and evaluation jobs run by the research side of the team, and ad-hoc experimentation. The inference service has hard latency requirements — p95 under 400ms — and it is the workload we cannot compromise. Research jobs, by contrast, are batch-shaped and can tolerate queueing, but in practice they queue badly because they compete with inference for the same cards with no meaningful priority discipline.

The result is a familiar pattern: inference sits idle at 2am while a fine-tuning job waits for a morning slot someone manually reserved, and researchers complain that experiments that should take an afternoon take three days. Meanwhile, finance sees a fleet that is two-thirds idle and reasonably asks why we're asking for more.

**Cost**

A new node of comparable capability would cost approximately $180k upfront plus meaningful power, cooling, and rack space, and it would depreciate over three to four years — a real annualised cost of $60–70k before we account for the operational overhead of managing it. Against that, the utilisation work is mostly engineering time we already control: perhaps four to six weeks of one senior engineer, plus some of my own attention. Even under generous assumptions about that engineer's fully-loaded cost, the improvement path is an order of magnitude cheaper for the capacity it is likely to unlock. If we can lift fleet utilisation from 38% to 65%, we have effectively added four cards' worth of capacity for the price of a scheduling layer and some discipline.

**Latency**

The risk on the utilisation path is that tighter packing of workloads degrades inference latency. This is a real risk and the central technical challenge. The mitigation is a proper priority and partitioning scheme: inference gets guaranteed headroom and preemption rights, batch work fills the gaps. Modern serving stacks support this reasonably well, but it requires careful load testing before we trust it. We should treat any regression in p95 latency as a hard stop and roll back.

**Reliability**

Buying more hardware does add redundancy — one more node means a single-node failure is less catastrophic. But our reliability problems today are mostly self-inflicted: manual reservations that outlive their usefulness, jobs that silently hold memory, and no automated failover between cards. Fixing these improves reliability on the current fleet and would carry over to any future fleet. Buying hardware without fixing the operational discipline would simply give us a larger system to mismanage.

**Opportunity cost**

The utilisation work consumes senior engineering time that could otherwise go to product features. That is the honest trade-off. However, the alternative — buying hardware — consumes capital and also consumes engineering time in provisioning, integration, and ongoing maintenance, while leaving the underlying scheduling dysfunction intact. We would be paying twice: once in dollars and once in the same engineering attention, to solve a problem we could have solved more cheaply.

**Reversibility**

This is where the utilisation path is decisively stronger. Scheduling improvements, quota systems, and monitoring are software: they can be adjusted, reverted, or superseded. A purchased node is a commitment with a multi-year depreciation tail, and if demand shifts — a model architecture change, a shift to a hosted API for some workloads, a product pivot — that capital is sunk. Buying is not irreversible in the way a lease of office space is, but it is sticky enough that we should be confident before we commit.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be candid about what we don't know. Our utilisation numbers come from coarse monitoring and may understate true contention; it's possible the fleet is more genuinely saturated during the hours that matter than our averages suggest. Demand growth is also uncertain — if the research roadmap lands two large fine-tuning campaigns next quarter, even a well-scheduled fleet may be insufficient. And there is a chance the engineering effort to build fair preemption across our mixed workloads proves harder than estimated.

**Decision and next steps**

We propose a time-boxed effort: build the priority scheduler, instrument utilisation properly, and re-measure in eight weeks. If peak-hour inference latency holds and research queue times drop materially, we defer purchase. If not, we will return with a concrete sizing request grounded in measured demand rather than anxiety. Either outcome leaves us better informed, and neither burns the capital we may genuinely need later.
